His record was 4–6, but his ERA was a sparkling 2.08. He is also remembered for running the wrong way on the bases. He died at the age of 54 in Butte, Montana, on June 12, 1937. The left-hander batted right-handed, but manager Frank Selee suggested he try batting left-handed. When he made contact with the ball, he was confused enough to run to third base (he was thrown out at first base)

name: Basil Al Bayati
train_texts: Basil Al Bayati is an Iraqi-born architect and designer. He is considered to be one of the most important names in Metaphoric Architecture. He has also designed furniture and artistic pieces for the household. He currently resides in Málaga in the South of Spain where he runs a successful architectural practice and cultural centre as well as continuing his writing. His work is manifested in plans and publications that express an exuberance for visual forms rare in the Arab world today. His projects encompass a wide variety of architectural possibilities and transcend generally accepted patterns. In all of his buildings an organic obsession with flower forms and old Islamic symbolism has been merged into a fantastic alternative architecture for the future.

name: Wolfgang Unzicker
train_texts: Wolfgang Unzicker was one of the strongest German chess Grandmasters from 1945 to about 1970. He won the German Championship six times from 1948 to 1963 and tied for first in 1965. He played in twelve Chess Olympiads, and was first board on ten of them. His brother, four years older, was also a chess player but was killed in World War II. He decided against making chess his profession, choosing law instead. For many years he was legal advisor for the German Chess Association. He died on 20 April 2006 at the age of 86. He is survived by his wife, Barbara, and their three children. Unzicker had a classical chess style modelled after the German player and theorist Siegbert Tarrasch. In 1956 he lost a match to Paul Keres in which both players chose to begin with the Ruy Lopez opening in all eight games. In 2005, Unzicker celebrated his 80th birthday with his wife Freia, his three sons and their wives and three grandchildren, and a tournament with Karpov,  Korchnoi and  Spassky took place in his honor. He died on April 20, 2006, at the age of 80, during a holiday trip to Albufeira/Portugal.

name: Werner Wolff
train_texts: Werner Wolff was a German-born American photojournalist. He was one of the first to photograph Hitler's mountain retreat in Berchtesgaden after its capture by the Allies. Wolff photographed virtually everything, from famous (and not so famous) people to newsworthy events to technically challenging subjects. His work appeared in the pages of many publications, including Time, Life, Ebony and many others. He died in 2002 as a result of a long-term illness, leaving behind an enormous and rich portfolio. His photographs were donated to the Ryerson Image Centre in 2009 along with his negatives, contact sheets, tear sheets, and notebooks.

name: Giovanni Battista Zelotti
train_texts: Giovanni Battista Zelotti (1526 – 28 August 1578) was an Italian painter of the late Renaissance. He appears to have been born in Verona, then part of the Venetian mainland, and trained with Antonio Badile and Domenico Riccio. He was a contemporary of Paolo Veronese and shared work in the Villa Soranza near Castelfranco and at Venice. He frescoed villas designed by Andrea Palladio, notably Villa Emo and Villa Foscari, where he worked with Bernardino India and Battista Franco. He also worked in Mantua for the house of Gonzaga.

name: Adolph Modéer

As an economic historian, he wrote on the history of Sweden's trade. He also worked on jellyfish. His publications as a naturalist were: Någre märkvärdigheter hos insectet Cimex ovatus pallide-griseus, abdominis lateribus albo nigroque variis, alis albis, basi scutelli nigricante. name: Richard Sundeleaf
train_texts: Richard Wilhelm Sundeleaf was an American architect from Portland, Oregon. He trained in the Beaux Arts style of traditional design. He became known for his imaginative work in industrial architecture. He designed numerous residential and public buildings around Portland. He also designed many homes in Lake Oswego, Oregon, from 1940 until his death. In 1935 he designed a Tudor style English cottage for the University of Oregon chapter of Chi Psi in Eugene. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) in 1993. He died on March 8, 1987, at the age of 90. His designs include the Dr. Walter Black House, which is on the NRHP. Sundeleaf died on March 8, 1987, at his home in Lake Oswego. His career included over 3000 projects. With his wife, Mildred, he also owned a 160-acre (65 ha) ranch in southwestern Montana, acquired in 1956. He was married from 1925 until his death, to whom he was married to from 1925 to 1987. He is buried at the F. F. Murphy House, in Northwest Portland, Oregon, where he once lived with his wife Mildred. The Sundeleaf family also owns a home in Montana, which they bought in 1956, and a ranch in southwest Montana.

name: Gottlieb Burckhardt
train_texts: Johann Gottlieb Burckhardt (24 December 1836 – 6 February 1907) was a Swiss psychiatrist and the medical director of small mental hospital in the Swiss canton of Neuchâtel. He is commonly regarded as having performed the first modern psychosurgical operation. In 1888 he excised various brain regions from six psychiatric patients under his care. He believed that mental illnesses had their origins in specific regions of the brain. After the death of his wife in 1896 he returned to Basel where he established a sanatorium in 1900. He died seven years later from pneumonia in Basel, Swiss Canton, in 1907.
eval_texts: Johann Gottlieb Burckhardt (24 December 1836 – 6 February 1907) was a Swiss psychiatrist and the medical director of small mental hospital in the Swiss canton of Neuchâtel. Aimed at relieving symptoms rather than effecting a cure, the theoretical basis of the procedure rested on his belief that psychiatric illnesses were the result of specific brain lesions. He died seven years later from pneumonia at a sanatorium in Basel, Switzerland, where he had established a private practice in 1900.

name: Genrikh Kasparyan
train_texts: Genrikh Kasparyan was an Armenian chess player and composer. He won the Armenian championship ten times, including two ties with future World Champion Tigran Petrosian. He was awarded the titles of International Judge of Chess Compositions in 1956 and International Grandmaster of Chess Composition in 1972. He wrote several books and collections and composed about 600 studies, many on the theme of domination, winning 57 first prizes. He died in Yerevan, Armenia, in 1995 at the age of 87. His compositions include the pieces "The Art of domination" and "The Power of domination", both written in the early 20th century.

name: Leah Chase
train_texts: Leah Chase is a New Orleans chef, author and television personality. She is known as the Queen of Creole Cuisine, and advocates for African-American art and Creole cooking. Her restaurant, Dooky Chase, was known as a gathering place during the 1960s among many who participated in the Civil Rights movement. Chase was inducted into the James Beard Foundation's Who's Who of Food & Beverage in America in 2010. The Southern Food and Beverage Museum in New Orleans, Louisiana named a permanent gallery in Chase's honor in 2009. Chase received honorary degrees from Tulane University, Dillard University, Our Lady of Holy Cross College, Madonna College, Loyola University New Orleans and Johnson & Wales University.

name: Rob Slotemaker
train_texts: Rob Slotemaker was a Dutch racing driver. He entered one Formula One World Championship race, the 1962 Dutch Grand Prix, but his car was not ready in time for the event. Throughout the 1960s Slotemaker competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans race, and was a driver and advisor for the Le Mans film in 1970. In 1956 he established his anti-skid driving school at Zandvoort, which is still operating today. On 16 September 1979 he was killed when he crashed his Chevrolet Camaro during the Trophy of the Dunes touring car race. His car spun on a patch of oil and collided with a course car parked alongside the track. He suffered a broken neck and died instantly.

name: William F. Norrell
train_texts: William Frank Norrell was a U.S. Representative from Arkansas' former 6th congressional district. He was succeeded in Congress by his widow, Catherine Dorris Norrell. During World War I, Norrell served in the Quartermaster Corps of the United States Army. In 1920, he was admitted to the bar and commenced practice in Monticello in Drew County, Arkansas. From 1930 to 1938, he served as member of the Arkansas State Senate. He served as Senate President from 1934 to 1938 under Lieutenant Governors William Lee Cazort and Robert L. Bailey. He died in Washington, D.C. in 1961.

name: Bill Moisan
train_texts: William Joseph Moisan, Jr. (July 30, 1925 – April 9, 2010) was a pitcher in Major League Baseball who played briefly for the Chicago Cubs during the 1953 season. Listed at 6 ft 1 in (1.85 m), 170 lb., he batted left-handed and threw right-handed. A decorated veteran of World War II, Moisan was stationed at Fort Benning, Georgia, and then Fort Bragg, North Carolina, before going overseas with Company G of the 398th Infantry Regiment, 100th Infantry Division. He served in France in 1944, and was part of the Allied advance into Germany in May 1945, earning the Silver Star at Jagstfeld. Moisan played for the Los Angeles Angels from 1950 to 1953. He had a 98–96 record with a 3.81 ERA in 329 games, 135 as a starter. A .222 lifetime hitter, he enjoyed his best season in 1953, posting career numbers in average (.284), runs (15), hits (40), home runs (four), RBI (23), OBP (.327) and SLG (.418) During his time with the LA Angels he was once the roommate of actor and professional athlete Chuck Connors. He also served as the nuclear materials manager at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, retiring in 1985. Moisan died in Brentwood, New Hampshire, at the age of 84.

name: John James Joass
train_texts: John James Joass was a Scottish architect, born in Dingwall, Scotland. Joass joined John Belcher's practice in 1896, and became a partner in 1905. He was also joint architect of Whiteleys department store, which opened in 1911, and the re-building of the Swan and Edgar department store after 1920. He retired to Poole, Dorset sometime after 1930, and was an avid sailor of small sailing craft. He died in Poole on 10 May 1952, at the age of 83. He is buried in the John Burnet Memorial Cemetery in Glasgow. His father William Cumming Joass had been an established architect in that town.

train_texts: Ellsworth Young (1866 Albia, Iowa – 1952 Evanston, Illinois) was an American magazine and book illustrator, and a noted painter of landscapes. He painted several posters for the war effort of World War I, his best-known probably being \"Remember Belgium\". In 2010 Western Illinois University began looking at stored works of art to refurbish, and discovered a rolled-up painting which held “tremendous historical significance” It was a painting by Young of a river landscape in autumn, and had been commissioned in 1934 to hang in Monroe Hall (later known as Grote Hall) and remaining there for some 60 years until the Hall was demolished in 1991.

name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
train_texts: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was a German-American architect. Along with Le Corbusier, Walter Gropius and Frank Lloyd Wright, he is widely regarded as one of the pioneers of modernist architecture. Mies sought to establish a new architectural style that could represent modern times just as Classical and Gothic did for their own eras. His mature buildings made use of modern materials such as industrial steel and plate glass to define interior spaces. He strove toward an architecture with a minimal framework of structural order balanced against the implied freedom of unobstructed free-flowing open space. He is often associated with his quotation of the aphorisms, \"less is more\" and \"God is in the details''

train_texts: Paul England was an Australian former racing driver. He raced his own 138 Holden-powered grey motor Ausca sports racing car. England contested a single Formula One World Championship Grand Prix race, the 1957 German Grand Prix, in a Formula Two Cooper T41-Climax. After retiring from racing, England owned a general engineering company called Paul England & Staff in Essendon, Victoria, Australia. In the 1970s England's company built 1.6 litre Ford engines for motor racing which were referred to as an England engine. Paul England died on 17 June 2014 at the age of 87. He was the father of Lisa Mary Coulton and her husband Steven Coulton.

name: Harmon Elwood Kirby
train_texts: Harmon Elwood Kirby was an American diplomat, U.S. Ambassador to Togo, and Foreign Service Officer. He was married, had two children, and resided in Bethesda, Maryland. Kirby received his Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree from Harvard University. He also received his Master of Arts degree from George Washington University. He was one of only six physicians summoned to Rome to consult about the treatment of Pope John Paul II when he was shot in 1981. "His intelligence, diligence, attention to detail, restraint leavened with generosity, caring and a touch of humor brought him the trust of his peers and a succession of assignments," said the AMA. "He truly characterizes him as one of the great surgical statesmen America has produced.”
